name: Azithromycin pulse (acne)
lead: Azithromycin pulse dosing for acne refers to the use of the oral macrolide antibiotic azithromycin in short, intermittent courses (for example on a few days each week) as a treatment for inflammatory acne vulgaris. It is an off-label dermatology practice in many countries; azithromycin is a prescription-only antibiotic, and the pulse schedule is a prescriber's decision rather than a product category.[1][2]

Azithromycin was discovered in 1980 by the Zagreb pharmaceutical company Pliva, approved for medical use in 1988, and launched by Pfizer as Zithromax in 1991. It binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and has a long tissue half-life of about 68 hours, which is the pharmacological basis for short or intermittent courses.[1]

Evidence for the acne use consists mainly of small registered trials comparing azithromycin with doxycycline, minocycline, or add-on agents such as probiotics, levamisole or light therapy.[3][4][5][6][7] The general acne literature notes that dermatologists prefer antibiotics in combination with non-antibiotic agents and that resistant Cutibacterium acnes strains, including to macrolides, have increased.[8]

paras: Oral antibiotics are a standard option for moderate inflammatory acne. Commonly listed agents are tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline), with erythromycin and other macrolides used less often.[8] Azithromycin is not discussed in the general acne overview cited here; its use is typically a clinician's choice, for instance when tetracyclines are unsuitable.

Pulse regimens give the drug on set days rather than daily, relying on its accumulation in tissues and phagocytes and long half-life.[1] Specific schedules are set by prescribers and are not described here.

As a macrolide, azithromycin blocks bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit.[1] C. acnes, a skin bacterium implicated in acne inflammation through TLR2 and TLR4 signalling, is the main bacterial target of acne antibiotics.[8]

Common adverse effects of azithromycin are diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain and vomiting; fewer than 1% of patients stop treatment because of them. C. difficile infection, hearing loss, allergic reactions and liver effects have been reported.[1]

In 2013 the US FDA warned that azithromycin can prolong the QT interval and lead to torsades de pointes, particularly in people with existing QT abnormalities, low potassium or magnesium, or slow heart rate.[1]

Acne guidance generally recommends limiting oral antibiotic courses to about three months and avoiding antibiotic monotherapy, because heavy use has increased resistant C. acnes strains, including to macrolides.[8]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists several registered acne trials of azithromycin: a 2006 phase 2 comparison with doxycycline (n=100)[3]; a phase 3 trial of sustained-release azithromycin versus minocycline (terminated, n=118)[5]; a phase 2/3 trial of azithromycin with or without levamisole (n=169)[7]; azithromycin versus azithromycin plus probiotics (a 2025 phase 4 trial, n=60)[2]; azithromycin versus probiotics (n=75)[6]; azithromycin plus 308-nm excimer light (n=32)[4]; and a vitamin A plus azithromycin study (n=30).[9] The registry records cited here do not report outcome data, so this article does not state their results.
Pulse azithromycin appears on lists of antibiotic options discussed for acne alongside doxycycline and minocycline. No community sources are cited here, and reported experiences vary by individual.

card.summary: Short intermittent courses of an oral macrolide antibiotic used off-label for inflammatory acne; evidence is small head-to-head trials and resistance is a stated concern.
card.note: Prescription antibiotic; QT prolongation warning and antibiotic-resistance concerns.

quick.overview:
Azithromycin is a prescription macrolide antibiotic. Some prescribers use it in intermittent 'pulse' courses for inflammatory acne, often as an alternative to tetracycline-class antibiotics.

Published support consists mostly of small registered trials against doxycycline or minocycline or with add-ons such as probiotics; the registry records cited do not report outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It blocks bacterial protein synthesis and accumulates in tissues with a half-life of about 68 hours, which is why short or intermittent courses are used. The bacterial target in acne is Cutibacterium acnes.
quick.risks: Common effects are gastrointestinal. The FDA has warned about QT prolongation, and acne guidance cautions that repeated antibiotic exposure has increased resistant C. acnes, generally recommending courses of no more than about three months.
